newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire accuses Uganda of border attack.
newsitem.headline: Zaire accuses Uganda of border attack.

text.p: Zaire accused Uganda on Sunday of attacking its territory around the eastern town of Kasindi as the conflict gripping the Great Lakes region of Central Africa looked set to widen.
"The Ugandans attacked Zairean army positions at Kasindi," Zairean Information Minister Boguo Makeli told Reuters.
"They have tried to justify the attack saying they were using their right to pursue elements from the Uganda Democratic Party."

A senior Ugandan official confirmed to Reuters that Ugandan forces had shelled positions held by rebels near Kasindi but denied a report by an official Ugandan newspaper that Ugandan troops had crossed the border and seized the town on Thursday.
Buguo said later on state television that Zaire would hit back.
"We will respond. But one cannot launch a counter-attack without being sure where that will lead," he said.

Uganda's government newspaper, New Vision, said on Saturday that Ugandan troops crossed into eastern Zaire on Thursday to attack Ugandan rebel bases. It said 23 rebels were killed when the army seized Kasindi and the surrounding Virunga hills.
Kasindi is about 10 km (six miles) west of Zaire's border with Uganda.
"We are fed up with these bandits. We are going to finish them," Ugandan Lieutenant-Colonel Geoffrey Muheesi was quoted as saying by New Vision. He said his soldiers would not leave the area.
He accused Zaire of equipping the rebels, who have been raiding western Uganda. The Zairean government has denied this.
The Zairean minister said Zairean military reinforcements had been sent to the area of Beni, about 55 km (35 miles) northwest of Kasindi.

This new region of conflict lies just north of where an alliance of Zairean rebels backed by Uganda and Rwanda are fighting Zairean government troops and forces of Rwanda's former Hutu government which was driven into Zaire in 1994.
The fighting has displaced over one million Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees as well as unknown numbers of local Zaireans.
Zaire denied last week that the town of Butembo, some 40 km (25 miles) south of Beni, had fallen to Zairean rebels and that rebels were advancing up the road north.
But Boguo could not say whether Butembo had fallen or not.
"The situation there is very confused. The population have fled the town but we cannot deduce from that that Butembo has been taken," he said.
Boguo denied that Zaire was in contact with or supporting Ugandan rebels said by the government of President Yoweri Museveni to have bases on Zairean soil.

The Kinshasa government says Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila, whose forces hold a strip of eastern Zaire, is a puppet in the hands of a coalition of ethnic Tutsi forces from Rwanda and Burundi, supported by Uganda.

Uganda's Museveni has close ties with Rwandan military strongman, Vice President and Defence Minister Paul Kagame, whose Tutsi rebel forces drove Hutu government forces out of Rwanda in 1994 after their genocide of an estimated one million minority Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
